newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's DIHT sees modest export-led recovery.
newsitem.headline: Germany's DIHT sees modest export-led recovery.

text.p: Germany's Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT) said on Tuesday that its autumn survey of 25,000 companies pointed to a modest upturn in the German economy next year.

However, the DIHT forecast of 1.5 to two percent growth in 1997 shows business leaders are less optimistic than the Bonn government and leading think-tanks, which have projected 2.5 percent growth in the coming year.
The positive outlook could deflate without sustained progress toward the broad economic reforms the governing is trying to push through, the industry-based organization warned.
"The easing of the economic climate must be supported by political signals," DIHT head Franz Schoser told reporters.

"The serious discussion of a radical income tax reform shows that the political forces want to reduce the structural costs of doing business in Germany. This goal must not be tied up in political manoeuvring."
The DIHT said the mark's fall against the dollar had boosted exports, as had expansion by German companies into the growing markets of Asia and Central Europe.
Based on its September survey, the DIHT projected export growth of five percent next year, a point higher than its forecast in the autumn of 1995.

"The central hope for economic growth in 1997 in Germany will be exports," Schoser said. "In view of the stagnating domestic market, companies have strengthened their overseas efforts. They have made improvements in their competitiveness."
West German industrial, retail and service companies expect an improved climate in 1997, while the construction sector and east German companies will remain weak, the DIHT said.
Of west German firms, 23 percent expect business to improve in 1997, up from 18 percent a year ago. Only 26 percent see conditions worsening, down from 34 percent last fall.
More than half -- 51 percent -- expect conditions to remain the same. A year ago, 48 percent saw no change in west Germany.

In east Germany, 22 percent expect better business in the coming year, the same percentage as in the DIHT poll last year. Twenty-three percent see a worsening, down from 27 percent last year. Fifty-five percent see no change, compared to 51 percent in the autumn 1995 survey.
The business climate in eastern Germany has reached a new low, with a slump in construction depriving the economy of drive, Schoser said.
Germany will continue to see a negative investment flow in 1997 because of the high cost of doing business in Germany.
"Domestic investment remains the weak point in the business climate," Schoser said.
Similarly, he said the brightening of the economic outlook would have no positive impact on overall employment.
"In contrast to the economic forces, a further reduction in the work force in industry must be expected," Schoser said.
